## Conclusion

The evidence supports your claim: bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR is associated with greater survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) than no bystander CPR. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 72 studies encompassing nearly 3 million OHCA cases found that bystander CPR significantly improved survival—44% higher odds of survival to hospital discharge and 50% higher odds of favorable neurologic survival compared with no bystander CPR [1]. The American Heart Association’s science advisory concluded that hands-only CPR produces survival outcomes similar to conventional CPR with rescue breaths, and recommended hands-only CPR for lay bystanders to reduce barriers to action [2]. The landmark SOS-KANTO observational study (Lancet 2007) showed that bystander chest-compression-only CPR was associated with higher rates of neurologically favorable survival than conventional CPR among witnessed adult OHCA [3]. A 2025 systematic review similarly concluded that bystander CPR remains the most important modifiable factor improving OHCA survival [4]. Collectively, these data indicate that hands-only CPR is at least as effective as conventional CPR and substantially better than no CPR, supporting public health campaigns promoting hands-only CPR for witnessed adult cardiac arrest.
